approachQuestion.prompt: Roll exactly d distinguishable dice in order. Each die has faces numbered 1 through f. Return the number of ordered face sequences whose sum is T, modulo 1000000007. Examples: d=2,f=3,T=4 → 3 ([1,3],[2,2],[3,1]); d=1,f=6,T=0 → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ d ≤ 30; 1 ≤ f ≤ 30; 0 ≤ T ≤ 1000. Return only the modular count.

options.text: Use one row for sums after the preceding number of dice and one zeroed current row. Initially only sum zero has count one. For each die and each sum s=0..T, add previous[s−v] over faces v=1..f with v≤s, modulo the modulus. Swap row references.
options.feedback: The state includes how many dice have been used. Each last face leads to a count with exactly one fewer die; resetting the current row prevents counts from different die counts leaking together.

options.text: Use the same exact-dice recurrence but retain rows for all die counts through d.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: Keep only one sum array and repeatedly update sums upward for each face, without tracking the number of dice.
options.feedback: For d=1,f=2,T=2, this can include [1,1], though exactly one die allows only [2].

options.text: Count unordered multisets of d faces totaling T.
options.feedback: For d=2,f=3,T=4, [1,3] and [3,1] are separate rolls; merging them gives two instead of three.

feedback.reason: Keep an exact resource-count dimension and initialize the zero-resource empty construction correctly.
details: Allocate two arrays of T+1 counters. Start previous[0]=1. For every one of d dice, zero the current row, scan all s=0..T, and loop v=1..f, adding a preceding-row entry only when v≤s. Do not skip the face loop for impossible sums; swap references.

The preceding row represents exactly one fewer die, so face choices preserve ordered distinguishable rolls. The fixed loops check every face even for impossible sums; do not infer a faster implementation by skipping them.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Allocate two arrays of T+1 counters. Start previous[0]=1. For every one of d dice, zero the current row, scan all s=0..T, and loop v=1..f, adding a preceding-row entry only when v≤s. Do not skip the face loop for impossible sums; swap references. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=d; d,f,T vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: Count d*(T+1)*f specified face checks and two retained sum rows.
details: The specified loops perform d(T+1)f face checks, including rejected faces. Zeroing rows and initialization are dominated because d,f≥1. Two T+1-entry rows are retained, with no output sequences or recursion.
“O(d(T+1)) time, O(T+1) auxiliary space”: The fixed loops check all f faces for every sum and die. They do not replace that loop with a running window sum.
“O(d(T+1)f) time, O(d(T+1)) auxiliary space”: Only two rows survive; the method does not retain a row for each die count.
“O(d+T+f+1) time, O(T+1) auxiliary space”: The nested die, sum, and face loops multiply their work rather than add it.
